## When AI infrastructure outgrows the storage beneath it


AI infrastructure is often measured in GPUs, network bandwidth and compute density. But for many AI and high-performance computing environments, the limiting factor is not the accelerator. It is the storage architecture feeding it.


As datasets grow and workloads become more distributed, infrastructure teams need storage that can sustain high throughput, support frequent checkpoints, remain available through component or node failures and fit within increasingly constrained power and space envelopes. They also need an architecture that can be deployed and supported without being locked into a proprietary stack.


That is the conversation Celestica is bringing to AI Infra Summit 2026 in Santa Clara. Across the event, Celestica will highlight its[networking](https://www.celestica.com/our-expertise/platform-solutions/networking) and[storage controller](https://www.celestica.com/our-expertise/platform-solutions/storage) portfolio, along with the design, integration and lifecycle capabilities needed to move from individual components to production-ready infrastructure.


The most detailed example will come from[a real-world AI and HPC deployment: the Helma supercomputer at the Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) in Germany.](https://www.celestica.com/uploadedFiles/Site/our-expertise/platform-solutions/case-studies/Xinnor_Case_Study.pdf)


## A production blueprint for high-performance, highly available storage


Celestica and Xinnor have partnered to create a blueprint of a solution that can provide highly available storage for modern AI workloads.Together, they have addressed the storage bottlenecks in one of Germany’s largest university supercomputing environments. Most recently, they collaborated on the Helma deployment, one of the most powerful university-owned AI supercomputers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) in Germany.


The core blueprint for the Helma deployment combines Celestica SC6100 PCIe Gen5 all-flash storage controllers with Xinnor’s xiRAID software and an open Lustre file system—bringing hardware and software together into one high-availability operating architecture.


The Helma deployment was built to serve768 GPUs with a 5PB highly available, all-NVMe Lustre storage cluster. Ten Celestica SC6100 systems provide the hardware foundation, with each system using dual server nodes and shared PCIe Gen5 NVMe storage. Xinnor xiRAID provides the software RAID layer and failover capabilities.


The result is a storage architecture designed around the realities of AI and HPC: sustained data movement, resilience during failures, serviceability and efficient use of data center resources.


## What the Helma use case shows technical buyers


The value of this architecture is not simply that it uses fast NVMe drives. The more important lesson is how the system is designed to keep the entire workload moving.


### **1. GPU utilization depends on the full data path**


A high-performance GPU cluster can only deliver its potential when storage can supply data and absorb checkpoints at the required rate. In the Helma environment, the Celestica SC6100 controllers, PCIe Gen5 NVMe media, Xinnor xiRAID and Lustre file system were combined to reduce the risk that storage would become the limiting resource.


The published results illustrate the impact: the solution achieved 1,798.77 GiB/s in IOR Easy Read performance and more than 8.2 million IOPS in metadata testing. It also reached the number-three position in the[global IO500 benchmark](https://io500.org/) and the number-one position among Lustre-based solutions.


### **2. High availability has to be designed in from the beginning**


For long-running AI training, scientific simulation and research workloads, a drive or server failure can create more than a short interruption. It can waste compute cycles, delay experiments and force teams to repeat work.


The Helma architecture uses dual-node redundancy in the SC6100 systems and xiRAID failover capabilities to support continued operation through drive and node failures. That makes high availability part of the storage design rather than an operational patch applied later.


### **3. Density changes the economics of scale**


The Helma solution delivered this performance in a half-rack footprint—roughly one-tenth the size of many competing multi-rack appliances described in the published case study. A smaller physical footprint can reduce the associated demands on power, cooling and data center space while supporting high-density AI infrastructure.


For organizations expanding AI capacity, those system-level economics matter. The goal is not only to increase peak performance; it is to maximize workload performance per rack, per watt and per dollar of infrastructure investment.


### **4. Open integration creates a more flexible path to production**


The Helma stack combines open hardware and open-source components, including AlmaLinux and Lustre, with Xinnor’s proprietary xiRAID software. That approach gives infrastructure teams more flexibility to select the right technologies for their workloads while avoiding the assumption that performance requires a fully closed appliance.


It also creates a repeatable blueprint. The question for technical buyers is not whether one exceptional system can achieve strong benchmark results. It is whether the architecture can be adapted, integrated and supported for the next AI or HPC environment.


## From scientific research to broader AI workloads


The Helma use case is rooted in scientific and academic computing, including deep learning for physics simulations, biomedical image analysis and materials science. The same storage requirements appear in other data-intensive environments: large language model training, multilingual translation, computer vision, robotics and reinforcement learning, and AI-assisted engineering and smart manufacturing.


In each case, infrastructure leaders are balancing the same questions: How do we keep accelerators supplied with data? How do we maintain service through failures? How do we scale without multiplying footprint and operational complexity? And how do we preserve flexibility as workloads, processors and storage media evolve?
